sentences.text: Eddie Lever was able to leave his tenancy more easily because of the Renters' Rights Act When the Renters' Rights Act came into force in May it was described as the biggest change for tenants in England in a generation, giving more stability and security to the millions of people who rent from private landlords.

sentences.text: The legislation has also prompted a shake-up of the student rental market, which has posed challenges for landlords as it allows people to leave a tenancy rather than being tied in for the full academic year.

sentences.article_title: Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents

sentences.article_title: Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents

sentences.text: The legislation ended fixed-term tenancies - where renters are tied in to contracts for a specific number of months.
sentences.article_title: Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents

sentences.text: For students, previously contracts were generally for the full academic year.
sentences.article_title: Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents

sentences.article_title: Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents

sentences.text: Ethan has wanted to be a paramedic from a young age When aspiring paramedic Ethan ordered three resuscitation manikins so he could teach CPR to others, he had no idea how quickly he would put his training into practice and help save a life.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: Just two weeks after the dummies arrived at his home in Mansfield Woodhouse, in Nottinghamshire, the 15-year-old found himself performing CPR on a man he found collapsed in the street.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: Ethan, who had completed a one-off CPR course with East Midlands Ambulance Service (EMAS) last year, said he went through "a million and one emotions" as he realised he was about to apply his knowledge to a real-life emergency.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: "It was adrenaline like never before, but I knew I had to stay calm, and not think too hard about the immense pressure of putting someone's life in your hands," he added.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: The teenager was on his way home from a casual gardening job at about 14:30 BST on 18 September when he saw a 75-year-old man slumped over "half in the road and half on the pavement" on Ley Lane.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: Ethan described the man as being unresponsive with a "raspy-sort of breathing" known as agonal breathing, and he was in cardiac arrest.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: Having completed his course with EMAS, and watching countless TV programmes about front-line emergency workers, Ethan's training kicked in.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: Ethan, a Year 10 pupil at The Manor Academy, said a lady who was on the phone to 999 was happy for him to take control as she did not know how to do chest compressions.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: Together, they moved the man to a safe, flat surface, where Ethan knew the CPR would be more effective.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: He said: "Even though I've spent ages preparing for this moment, to put it into practice was completely different." Ethan was soon joined at the scene by an off-duty carer from King's Mill Hospital and a teacher from a nearby primary school, who took turns with the compressions.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: He said it was a "massive sense of relief" when the paramedics arrived and prepared a defibrillator, and he felt a sense of hope once he saw the man had a "shockable rhythm".
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: According to Resuscitation Council UK (RCUK), an expert organisation on resuscitation, survival rates for cardiac arrests outside hospital "remain low", with one in 13 people surviving in the East Midlands.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: The organisation said the statistic highlighted a need to improve confidence in CPR and using defibrillators in the region.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: Ethan told the BBC he was thrilled to hear from the man's family that he was making a steady recovery.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: The man who Ethan helped wishes to remain anonymous while he continues his recovery but his daughter, Erica, said: "As a family, we are so grateful for the bravery that Ethan showed and our gratitude for assisting saving his life.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: "If it wasn't for Ethan and other passing public, there would have been a very different outcome.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: He bought the £60 resuscitation manikins with the aim of running free life-saving sessions, particularly for young people, and has already led training at local scout groups.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: He believes young people are reluctant to learn CPR because they feel awkward about "putting their hands on someone else".
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: He said: "There needs to be awareness that people performing CPR are protected by the Sarah Act." The Sarah Act is also known as the the Social Action, Responsibility and Heroism Act 2015, which is designed to protect people who help others or intervene in emergencies.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: Robert Gladwin, head teacher of The Manor Academy, said he would now look at investing some money to help more pupils learn life-saving skills.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: He added: "Quite often young people get a bad reputation but, actually, this shows we generate students who have a real community value.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: He added: "We would encourage people of all ages to learn CPR and how to use a defibrillator.
sentences.article_title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

sentences.text: "As Ethan's experience shows, having the confidence to act in an emergency could help save a life." sentences.text: This video can not be played Videographer Rhys Morgan captured footage of the world's second largest whale  lunge feeding This is the moment the planet's second largest living creature opens its giant jaws and swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding.
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: The fin whale was filmed by videographer Rhys Morgan off the Pembrokeshire coast in Wales, and it shows the mammal's expandable pleats take in up to 18,000 gallons of water and krill.
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: Morgan said "it was complete luck" that he captured the whale feeding and swimming with dolphins on his drone while fishing with a friend.
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: Second only to the blue whale, the fin whale is one of the largest animals ever to have lived, reaching up to 24m in length and weighing up to 70 tonnes.
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: Despite its enormous size, the fast-swimming creature is elusive and spends much of its life in the open ocean and often surfacing only briefly before disappearing beneath the waves.
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: The mammal can be found all over the world's oceans but is most at home in cooler waters.
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: "It's pretty incredible really," Morgan said.
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: "There's been times when we've been anchored up fishing with nothing happening in the area and a whale has popped up next to us.
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: "The wildlife will approach you sometimes." Dr Marianna Chimienti is a lecturer in marine top predator ecology at Bangor University and said Morgan experienced a "rare and fortunate encounter".
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: Chimienti, who specialises in animal behaviour added: "It is normal that the fin whale comes and feeds at the surface, as it is part of the species foraging strategy but being in the coastal water is quite spectacular.
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: "In theory, they should have migrated." Little is known about fin whale migration but their movements are believed to be quite different from other baleen whales such as blues and humpbacks.
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: Scientists have found that fin whales are more abundant in higher latitudes in warmer months of the year, and more numerous in lower latitudes during colder months, but this can vary.
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: Fin whales have a pretty simple diet which is usually made up of krill, small schooling fish and squid.
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: Due to the small size of its prey, fin whales have to eat a lot to survive and can spend several hours each day feeding, consuming up to 2,000 kilograms of food.
sentences.article_title: Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

sentences.text: Premier League managers beware.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: It's the last thing Manchester United boss Michael Carrick will want to read - as pressure piles on his future after Wednesday's Champions League humiliation in Como - but sacking season is just around the corner.

sentences.text: He won't be the only one looking anxiously over his shoulder, though.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: So far in this campaign, all 20 remain in situ.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: But when is the Premier League's 'sacking season'?
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: It doesn't make for good reading for those struggling managers.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: The most popular months for in-season managerial departures are November and December, with almost a third of all manager exits happening in these two months alone.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: Over the course of the competition's 34 completed seasons, there is a clear pattern of club boards opting for change around the autumn international breaks, and before Christmas and, crucially, the winter transfer window, which was introduced in England in 2003.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: Perhaps most ruthlessly of all, Charlton Athletic's Les Reed was dismissed on Christmas Eve in 2006, having won only one of his seven league games in charge, amassing four points.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: Reed's 40-day tenure was the shortest in Premier League history for almost two decades, until Sam Allardyce took that record in 2022-23 with a 30-day spell at Leeds United that ended in relegation.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: Ange Postecoglou lasted 39 days with Nottingham Forest last year.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: Among the high-profile managers to be shown the door in November are Chelsea 's Roberto di Matteo in 2012, Mauricio Pochettino at Spurs in 2019 and Manchester United playing legend Ole Gunnar Solskjaer in 2021.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: Di Matteo had spectacularly guided the Blues to FA Cup and Champions League success as caretaker boss six months earlier, but paid the price for a poor start in the defence of their European title.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: December has accounted for Jose Mourinho twice.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: In 2015 he departed reigning league champions Chelsea by mutual consent and in 2018 he was sacked by Manchester United .
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: Last season's average tenure of 310 days for departing managers was the second lowest on record in Premier League history.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: Only 1994-95 was lower, with an average of 154.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: Over the decades the patience of club owners has ebbed and flowed, with a notable dearth of sackings in 1995-96 and a more recent peak in longevity in 2021-22 that can largely be attributed to the pandemic.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: Since then, however, that patience seems to be wearing thin, with the average length of managerial reigns steadily plummeting.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: Postecoglou's brief stint at Forest last autumn was followed by a similarly short spell at Spurs for Igor Tudor, who picked up one point from five league games before being shown the door after 44 days.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: A record nine clubs entered this season with new permanent managers.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: Five of them are currently in the bottom half of the Premier League.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: With the grave financial consequences of relegation – and social media noise seemingly inescapable – clubs are showing no mercy when it comes to making big decisions.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: While no top-flight manager has been dismissed this season, there are several who will be looking over their shoulder before November's international break.
sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: But new Forest boss Oliver Glasner, and Sunderland 's Regis le Bris - whose side are juggling Europa League football - will be feeling a little bit anxious at the moment.

sentences.article_title: When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?

sentences.text: The fire burned through miles of moorland and woodland More than £1m is to be spent on nature recovery projects, including the restoration of habitats destroyed by a fire which ripped through a huge area of hillside in the Cairngorms.

sentences.text: The Scottish government funding will support habitat, species and river restoration, control of invasive non-native species and deer management across Scotland.

sentences.text: It includes £150,100 for recovery and nature restoration work following the Abernethy wildfire in the Cairngorms in July, to restore damaged habitats, help wildlife recover and reduce the risk of future wildfires.
sentences.article_title: Habitat destroyed by Cairngorms fire to be restored with government funding

sentences.text: Further funding will be provided to a range of other projects.
sentences.article_title: Habitat destroyed by Cairngorms fire to be restored with government funding

sentences.text: "This funding will support practical action, from improving habitats and rivers to tackling invasive species and supporting sustainable land management.
sentences.article_title: Habitat destroyed by Cairngorms fire to be restored with government funding

sentences.text: "Scotland is committed to turning its ambitions for nature and climate into action, both at home and on the international stage, and this investment will help deliver real benefits for our environment, wildlife and communities," she added.
sentences.article_title: Habitat destroyed by Cairngorms fire to be restored with government funding

sentences.text: "The funding announced today by Ms Martin is a very welcome boost that will help us to kickstart nature recovery in the area.
sentences.article_title: Habitat destroyed by Cairngorms fire to be restored with government funding

sentences.text: "From helping to manage land for chough on Islay to supporting the restoration of native oysters and creating meadows for wildlife in our towns and cities, these local efforts combine to create a national drive to save nature.
sentences.article_title: Habitat destroyed by Cairngorms fire to be restored with government funding

sentences.text: "And by working to restore biodiverse habitats, manage deer sustainably and tackle the invasive species that threaten our native animal and plant life, we can look forward with hope, to a future where Scotland's nature is healthy and thriving." sentences.text: Sam Fender said prices for his 2027 stadium tour would be lowered Sam Fender has called out the price of gig tickets ahead of his next tour, promising to lower the cost.

sentences.text: The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour earlier this week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester in summer 2027.

sentences.text: While tickets are yet to go on sale, Fender responded to a post on social media which claimed to outline the expected ticket prices.

sentences.text: The Geordie musician also said standing would not be split into a front and back tier and he had "no idea how this was normalised at gigs".

sentences.text: Tickets are due to go on general sale at 09:30 GMT on Friday, with a pre-sale at the same time on Wednesday.

sentences.text: But Fender said he was "not happy" with the reported prices.

sentences.text: "It got inflated well more than I'd had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on." The North Shields singer also said he did not want there to be an option for fans to pay more money to be closer to the front.

sentences.text: The George Inn, in Somerset, could hold the claim to the title of England's oldest pub Being England's oldest pub is a title claimed by a number of establishments across the country.
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: Pubs in Nottingham , St Albans and Lincolnshire have all, in the past, claimed to be that very establishment - but one pub in Somerset may have a stronger claim than its rivals.
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: The George Inn, in Norton St Philip , south of Bath, is the focus of that elusive claim of being the country's oldest pub - thanks to some investigative work by Historic England.
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: Buildings archaeologist Dr James Wright said science "pinpoints the archaeological development of the George Inn" to about 1430.
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: The 'most haunted' pubs and hotels where guests cannot explain encounters Long delays on M5 after lorry overturns Airbnb host fined as guests put at 'serious' risk The pub itself is Grade I listed and was constructed as a store for wool for the nearby Hinton Charterhouse.
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: It would also welcome travellers who attended the annual wool fairs which were held from the 13th Century until Victorian times.
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: Samuel Pepys (of Great Fire of London diarist fame) stopped there in 1668, describing it as "a very old house" and it also served as the headquarters for the Duke of Monmouth during the Monmouth Rebellion of 1685.
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: Its history then gets a little more grizzly because after the Duke's defeat, the pub became a court room for 'hanging judge' George Jeffreys who infamously condemned local rebels during the Bloody Assizes.
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: Dr James Wright said he thought scientific elements could help the pub's claim But none of that helps to verify the claim to the title of England's oldest pub - so what does?
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: Wright said, put simply, none of the other pubs possessed the archaeological evidence, archival references or scientific data "to actually back up the claims".
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: He said: "It's all about carefully placing all of the evidence together and working out in what order the real claimants go - and The George came out with the crown." Pub historian Charo Havermans agreed with that assertion.
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: "The strongest claims are when the history meets the science," she said.
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: "For example, tree ring dating can give us an idea of how old the timber or the wood used is.
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: "What we know about those times is that people wouldn't dilly dally so if they've cut down a tree, they're going to use it then," Havermans said.
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: "It's a pretty accurate way of knowing when the building materials were used to create that structure." Havermans also said historical records such as licensing data, local maps, or the Domesday Book could help date a pub.
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: However, we may never truly know where the oldest boozers are - a sentiment reinforced by Guinness World Records which has "rested" the accolade for the oldest pub since 2000, "when it became clear that it was not possible to verify it in full".
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: A spokeswoman for Guinness World Records said it was "never able to state definitively which was the oldest pub in the country, since the age and historical usage of buildings is, in many cases, uncertain".
sentences.article_title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?

sentences.text: The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: "AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: "I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: "One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country." The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: "That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: Don't leave AI to tech bros and oligarchs, UK's AI minister says The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional £120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: It will come alongside a £60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and £70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: It comes after the UK government revealed it was among organisations around the world to have taken some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.
sentences.article_title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

sentences.text: But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.

sentences.text: But recently the 22-year old has been strapping a camera to his head to record his work.

sentences.text: The camera only records his hands and fingers - his client's faces are blurred out.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "The routine is simple, but you have to be disciplined about how you move.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: The operations team taught me that my hands always have to stay cleanly inside the frame, the lighting has to be sharp, and I can't tilt my head too abruptly while working." He wears the camera for five or six hours a day.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "It's good money, but honestly, the feeling of doing something this futuristic is what keeps me excited.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: I never imagined my razor techniques would be useful to a global tech company," says Ashim.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: He is one of hundreds of thousands of workers across the world paid to record their activities.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: Ashim's footage is collected by a local company, which might have hundreds of people filming their work.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: That video is then sold on to technology companies and research organisations who use it to train artificial intelligence - in particular so-called physical AI, a type of artificial intelligence that can control robots in the real world.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: Rashdan Technologies collects and processes such human generated data.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "Every robotics company, every frontier AI lab, has a specific kind of data they want: industrial tasks, agriculture, household chores, small business work like pottery, garment-making, embroidery, candle-making.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: We go wherever the task is," says co-founder and CEO Shahil Baig.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: His company pays $5 to $10 (£3.74; £7.47) for eight to 10 hours of recorded work.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "For a lot of these people, that's meaningful," Baig says.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: Making sure workers give their consent and are comfortable with the process is important, he says.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "We record hands, not faces, and where multi-camera rigs do capture more of the body or environment, we blur faces out.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: No names, no contact details, nothing that identifies them personally goes into what we hand off." But his customers are getting more demanding.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "Now clients are asking for four to six cameras rigged around a person's head to cover the entire scene, not just the hands.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "Getting someone to agree to one small camera is one conversation.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: We pay more for that tier of data collection because of what we're asking of people." And the industry is becoming more crowded, Agarwal expects dozens more competitors to emerge in India this year.

sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: If you want robots to navigate the real world, they can't just be trained inside computer simulations, argues Manish Agarwal, the founder of Humyn Labs, which collects and processes human-generated data.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: Most of that data comes from video, but sometimes collectors wear hardware on their hands and fingers to capture physical contact.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "Physical tasks require high-quality signals involving limb movements, fingers, wrists, elbows, shoulders and dynamic force application.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: For example: applying the correct grip force so a plastic bottle doesn't crumble versus a steel glass," he says.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: And until recently, that data was not available.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "There is no existing internet archive of embodied human activity - no dataset of a kitchen being cleaned, or a car being assembled by hands that know exactly how much force to apply.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: That data has to be captured from scratch, in the real world, across diverse environments," says Agarwal, whose company has bases in Bangalore and San Francisco.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: At the moment his firm has 96,000 data collectors across countries in Latin America and Southeast Asia.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: Humyn Labs filters the thousands of hours of video supplied by those collectors, selecting the most useful content.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: It's then labelled so the AI knows what it is looking at and packaged in a format that can be used by clients.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "You need to source across a variety of factories, a variety of tasks, in different geographies because if you want to build deployment for US factories or US houses, you'd want environments that are a proxy for that.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: Residential houses in India may not be the right context for building a robotics use case for the US." This video can not be played The factory workers teaching robots how to work like humans But are workers collecting data for machines that will one day do their jobs?
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: At the moment it's too early to tell says Bino Paul, senior professor at the School of Management and Labour Studies at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) in Mumbai.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: For some workers AI might be a useful tool, but robots could automate other jobs, he says.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: The problem is that, if machines do start to take over, there will be little workers can do about.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "By the time workers realise what they have participated in, things may have gone too far," he says.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: Like many others, he wants governments to regulate AI.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "AI cannot be viewed merely as a technical system.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: We need to develop a socio-technical system in which ethics is upheld through human agency, ensuring that AI delivers beneficence rather than maleficence." Despite concerns over where AI is heading, money is still being poured into its development.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: Some of that trickles down to workers in India, where there is no shortage of workers prepared to wear a camera for a few dollars a day.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "Garments stitching and cutting.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: I know this work so well I could probably do it with my eyes closed.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: Cloth, thread, needle, machine after 10 years, your hands just know what to do before your mind even tells them," he says.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: He has recently started wearing a head-mounted camera that records his work.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: I have a family back home in Bihar, and every rupee I send back matters.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: If someone offers me extra money to wear a camera while I do the exact same work I've been doing for 10 years, I'm not going to say no.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: "It doesn't cost me anything.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: I'm already doing the stitching, already doing the cutting.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.text: But he argues the value of that kind of work will quickly become eroded, as more companies compete for collection contracts.
sentences.article_title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

sentences.article_title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?

sentences.text: Barb Hyman, founder of Sapia AI, said: "We don't know anything about you from a demographic perspective and we don't know whether or not you were hired or not hired for a previous role.
sentences.article_title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?

sentences.text: So I think you've really got to look at the nature of the AI and how it's built.
sentences.article_title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?

sentences.text: "At least in the enterprise space, every company we speak to is very conscious of the EU AI Act, even if they don't see themselves as having to comply with that yet.
sentences.article_title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?

sentences.text: And that requires a level of accountability." She added: "No company ever built a high-performing culture by monitoring its people, and you won't build a fair hiring process by policing candidates either.
sentences.article_title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?

sentences.text: "Start by earning candidates' trust: tell them what you're measuring, how they'll be scored, and give them feedback.
sentences.article_title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?

sentences.text: "We saw a huge uptick in applications, but strangely, they all look the same.
sentences.article_title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?

sentences.text: Our suspicion was candidates all of a sudden were using AI to make the applications themselves." Samways used two different AI tools to help the company understand how much of the content was produced by AI but they "produced such a variety of responses".
sentences.article_title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?

sentences.text: "We found we couldn't trust them and we had to literally sift through those, applications in a human way in the end.
sentences.article_title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?

sentences.text: "It's just clear that at this point we're not prepared to trust AI for this kind of decision-making." An ICO spokesperson said AI and automation could "make recruitment quicker and more efficient" but "must not come at the expense of people's rights".
sentences.article_title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?

sentences.text: They said: "Employers should be upfront about when automated decision-making is being used, how it works and how it could affect someone's application.
sentences.article_title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?

sentences.text: They added: "Existing legal protections, including equality and data protection law, already apply to AI systems, and we will act where additional protections are needed." There seems to be a real fear of the unknown because we are often unsure what happens on the other end once we click "apply".
sentences.article_title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?

sentences.text: But given it seems AI is here to stay, how can we ensure it's fair?
sentences.article_title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?

sentences.text: Anthony Lee and his wife Laura pleaded guilty at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday The Conservatives' former director of campaigning and his wife have received suspended prison sentences after they admitted to cheating at gambling by placing bets on the date of the 2024 general election.
sentences.article_title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets

sentences.text: Anthony Lee used "inside information" emerging from a private meeting called by then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak to bet on the general election date months before it took place, Southwark Crown Court heard.
sentences.article_title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets

sentences.text: Lee and his wife Laura stood to win more than £23,000 had their cheating not been uncovered, the court heard.
sentences.article_title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets

sentences.text: Lee was sentenced to 10 months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, while his wife was sentenced to four months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for a year.

sentences.text: Amy Hind, a former Tory party employee who was working as an NHS business support manager, was also sentenced to six months' imprisonment, suspended for a year, after previously pleading guilty to cheating on the date of the election.
sentences.article_title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets

sentences.text: Judge Tony Baumgartner, sentencing the three of them, said their conduct "risked undermining" the confidence the public has in the Conservative Party "as an institution", "undermining trust in the democratic process" and the "integrity of the gambling system".
sentences.article_title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets

sentences.text: The trio were among several people charged with betting offences by the Gambling Commission.
sentences.article_title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets

sentences.article_title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets

sentences.article_title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets

sentences.article_title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets

sentences.text: Baumgartner described Anthony Lee as a "central figure" in the preparation of the general election, who sat at a group of desks within Tory HQ known as the "God Pod".

sentences.text: Representing Lee, barrister Richard Pratt said his client did not concretely know the working date of the election, saying it "still represented a gamble from his point of view".

sentences.text: The barrister told the court: "It was always possible the prime minister could change his mind." Pratt said there "wasn't any direct manipulation" by the defendant.

sentences.text: Laura Lee worked for the Tories as their "head of international" and had been selected as the party candidate for Bristol North West for the election.

sentences.text: Duncan Parish told a conference in Lincolnshire on Wednesday there were "institutional challenges" within government that needed to be overcome to deliver change.
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: The Manchester office of Number 10 North - sister to London's Downing Street - was set up by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July.
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: Burnham's political opponents have called the office a "gimmick" and raised transparency concerns about the costs involved.
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: Speaking to the Great Exhibition conference of local political and business leaders, Parish said his career in the civil service to date had "not been without its frustrations" and there can be "friction" between different parts of government which have "similar but ever so slightly competing objectives".
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: Parish, a civil servant in Whitehall before moving to Manchester four years ago, said Number 10 North staff were "delivering outcomes at a national level across a huge range of areas" including health, transport, education and social care.
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: "But we continually need to work to overcome those institutional challenges," he added.
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: He said one priority of Number 10 North was to "shift power and accountability" closer to local areas, but acknowledged "that means reforming the civil service as well" - by not viewing national, regional and local government as separate.
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: "But to deliver that change, requires us all to change - and part of that change is a mindset shift within central government," he said.
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: In September, Conservative shadow minister Mike Wood raised concerns about "little information and so little transparency" surrounding Number 10 North which he described as a "gimmick".
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: "The minister either doesn't know or won't tell us how much No 10 North will cost, how many people work there or how many of them actually turn up to work - it's almost as though this hasn't been properly thought through," he told a House of Commons debate.
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: He called for the annual budget, staff levels and office attendance statistics to be published.
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: Current staffing levels have also not yet been clarified.
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson said last week that the government did not know how much has been spent on hotels for No 10 North staff, ministers and special advisers travelling between London and Manchester since it opened.
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: The cost is "not centrally collated" but is "being met within existing departmental budgets", Jameson said in response to a parliamentary question.
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: Number 10 North's latest summit of regional mayors, held in its "situation room", will take place on Thursday.
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: Burnham has previously indicated he will work there at least once a week, and hosted the Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in September .
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.text: Parish added in his speech: "How will we know if Number 10 North is working?
sentences.article_title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy

sentences.article_title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family

sentences.text: "A year or two added to a life sentence wouldn't make any difference to an offender.

sentences.article_title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family

sentences.text: Aleena, an aspiring lawyer, was murdered by Jordan McSweeney as she walked home from an east London bar in June 2022.
sentences.article_title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family

sentences.article_title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family

sentences.text: She added that the new measures would "bring accountability and rebalance the power in the justice system from offender to victim." Offenders who refuse to attend sentencing can already face a fine or up to two years additional imprisonment for contempt of court.
sentences.article_title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family

sentences.text: But the Ministry of Justice has acknowledged that longer jail time alone is unlikely to deter those already behind bars.
sentences.article_title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family

sentences.article_title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family

sentences.text: Judges will also be able to restrict social visits further to once every four weeks for a period of almost three months.
sentences.article_title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family

sentences.article_title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family

sentences.text: However, visits from prisoners' children will be exempt from the new sanctions.
sentences.article_title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family

sentences.article_title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family

sentences.article_title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family

sentences.text: That is what the government has told all of us to have on hand to get through a national emergency, as well as some other basic items.
sentences.article_title: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

sentences.text: Its "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need to get through a rocky few days.
sentences.article_title: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

sentences.text: On Friday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unexpected events "seem to becoming more common" and everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".
sentences.article_title: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

sentences.text: As one expert warns the UK is "light years" behind our neighbours when it comes to preparing for major disruption, we've drilled down into what you need and why.
sentences.article_title: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

sentences.text: The government recommends having enough supplies in the kitchen to last three days, including bottled water and non-perishable foods.
sentences.article_title: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

sentences.article_title: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

sentences.article_title: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

sentences.article_title: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

sentences.article_title: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

sentences.text: Private companies buying up care homes for older people in England could undermine the government's plan to create a universal care service , the regulator says.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: The Care Quality Commission's annual report , external highlights how a rising share of the care home market is owned by large firms - the five biggest increased their share by 26% in the last two years, driven by interest from US property investors, and now own one in seven homes.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: While there can be benefits, there are concerns the trend can lead to higher prices and a reduction in quality.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: The regulator said rapid changes to the market, including the fragmentation of home help into more smaller services, needed monitoring and clearer planning.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: The CQC said the changes to at-home care, which covers support to help people wash and dress, could create inefficiencies - nearly a third of these services are providing care to four or fewer people.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: In contrast, there are few smaller care homes judged important for providing specialist and personalised care.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: Small care homes have always represented a tiny proportion of the care home market, but over the last 14 years the numbers have fallen significantly, particularly those that combine care with nursing support, which are down by a quarter.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: The CQC said the funding system remains fragile – people using care services either self-fund or, for the poorest, the state helps to pay for their costs.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: And in some areas, providers are increasingly turning to self-funders, making it more difficult for councils to buy the care they need for those relying on state help.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: CQC chief inspector of adult social care Chris Badger said the reshaping of the market was happening "largely by accident rather than design", driven by a combination of economic pressure and the problems some councils were having in buying services for those relying on state-funded care.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: He said this government's renewed focus on social care – Andy Burnham made it one of his key priorities when he became prime minister – was welcome.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: But he said it was important the market was "shaped around what's best for people".
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: "A clearer vision is needed," he added.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: Hugh Alderwick, of the Health Foundation think-tank, said the report by the CQC "lays bare the massive challenges" facing the government.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: "The prime minister's commitment to reforming the sector provides an opportunity to fundamentally redraw the state's offer on social care.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: "But change is needed now to strengthen the fundamentals of the system.
sentences.article_title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says

sentences.text: "Unless we get some real progress in a funding settlement, the trend of smaller homes closing will be a trend that will continue." The Department of Health and Social Care said the report demonstrated the "scale of the challenge this government inherited", but said it was committed to overhauling social care.

sentences.text: A clinical trial has been launched in the UK which scientists hope could cut years from the search for new treatments for Alzheimer's disease.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: It will test multiple drugs simultaneously, starting with two repurposed medicines already used to treat type 2 diabetes and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: The study will examine whether the drugs can lessen symptoms such as memory and thinking problems, and help people maintain their quality of life.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: Angela Bucksey, 67, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in January and is the first person to begin treatment on the trial, called AD-SMART.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: "We have Alzheimer's in the family," she told the BBC.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: "My mother had it and my aunts, so it was a disappointment rather than a shock when I was diagnosed because I knew it would restrict my life.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: "But I was determined that it wasn't going to define me." Angela said she felt empowered joining the trial because "at least you are doing something".
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: "Instead of just sitting there, you're standing up and saying, I will fight back." Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, affecting around 600,000 people in the UK.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose father died from Alzheimer's last month, said he knew how it felt to lose a loved one to dementia, and had seen first-hand the devastating impact of the disease on families.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: "That's why I'm proud to see this trial being launched in the UK, so that cutting-edge treatments can reach patients here as soon as possible," he said.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: The AD-SMART study is what's known as a multi-arm, multi-stage platform trial where several treatments are tested simultaneously, with the results compared with one group of participants taking a placebo or dummy.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: This means those involved have a higher likelihood of getting an active treatment than in a traditional trial.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: If any drug isn't showing benefit it can be dropped quickly and a new treatment added in its place - the approach has been used successfully in cancer and motor neurone disease.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: The two initial drugs being tested are metformin, used to treat type 2 diabetes, and atomoxetine, for ADHD, which were selected by an international panel of experts.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: Both drugs may help reduce brain inflammation, which is a driver of neurodegeneration, said chief investigator Prof Paresh Malhotra, group leader at the UK Dementia Research Institute Centre for Care Research & Technology at Imperial College London.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: "For too long, Alzheimer's research has moved at the pace of one drug, one trial, one answer - sometimes taking a decade or more before we know if we've found something that works," he told the BBC.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: "We are applying advances from cancer and other conditions to accelerate testing of treatments for people with Alzheimer's disease." For the drugs to be successful, the study has to show that they have beneficial effects on thinking and the ability to carry out everyday activities.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: "That's what patients and their carers care about," said Prof Malhotra.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: Some 1,200 participants with mild to moderate Alzheimer's will be recruited at more than 30 sites across the UK.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: Sites in Cambridgeshire, Surrey, London, Southampton and Edinburgh are already open.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: Scientists expect to finish evaluating the first drugs in 2030 and, in that time, additional treatments are likely to be added.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: All the participants will have regular health checks including cognitive tests, which will help researchers assess how effective the treatments are.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: Angela Bucksey's husband Steve, who is her study partner, told the BBC: "Joining the trial has brought us back from the despair of a diagnosis which everybody recognises is non-recoverable.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: People with a confirmed Alzheimer's diagnosis who would like to take part can register their interest on the AD-SMART website , external .
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: The trial is being led by the UK Dementia Research Institute and Alzheimer's Research UK.
sentences.article_title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

sentences.text: Partners include the National Institute for Health and Care Research, the Medical Research Council and Health Data Research UK, with funding by UK government.

sentences.text: The sixth report of the Covid inquiry is highly critical of the way the government tried to protect people in care settings in the UK.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: Around 500,000 people were living in care homes at the start of the pandemic – with another million receiving care in their own homes.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: The inquiry said action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: Here are the key findings of the 287-page report.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: At the start of the pandemic, the then-health secretary in England, Matt Hancock, said the UK government had placed "a protective ring" around care homes.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: But the inquiry says this was not the case, listing a catalogue of failings.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: It says the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought".
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: A lack of personal protective equipment (PPE) meant staff had to resort to makeshift workarounds, including bin bags, festival waterproof ponchos and painters' overalls.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: The report is also critical of the way hospital patients who may be infected with Covid were moved to care homes to make space for others.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: The decision was understandable given the need to free up beds for Covid patients.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: But, without sufficient testing, it was important to keep these people separate and isolate them from others in case they were infected.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: Official guidance in March 2020 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland did not request this.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: That, the report says, was a significant oversight.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: When the pandemic started, high levels of staff vacancies and turnover in the social care sector meant that the workforce was "fragile and lacking resilience".
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: This undermined the ability of the sector to respond to the pandemic, the inquiry says.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: For example, care homes tend to rely heavily on agency staff who work in a variety of different homes.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: But a desire not to have staff going into multiple homes, to reduce the risk of infection transmission, meant staff shortages got even worse.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: Financially, care providers struggled too, as the number of people using services dropped.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: And for a sector that uses zero-hours contracts, there was a lack of financial support to help care staff stay off work if there was concern they might be infected.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: The response also suffered because of the fragmented nature of the system, with thousands of different providers and services overseen by councils.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: It meant the sector was more distant from government than the NHS.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: The pandemic, the inquiry said, exposed and exacerbated these existing weaknesses.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: The report is clear that precautionary steps taken to restrict visiting, as part of infection control, went too far.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: It acknowledges there was little choice to introduce bans on visitors at the start of the pandemic, saying that was rational.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: But as the pandemic progressed, so did the balance between the benefits and harms of restrictions.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: Visits are extremely important, allowing loved ones to help residents with everything from personal care to maintaining their mental health.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: By September 2020, evidence suggested visitors posed a "marginal risk" – staff were judged to be the key entry point for infections.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: The four UK nations then started to relax their guidance, but many care homes failed to implement this and visiting remained heavily restricted.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: This, says the inquiry, resulted in a significant decline in the health and wellbeing of residents.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation), including chest compressions, can be life-saving if a person's heart has stopped beating.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: But doctors can sometimes opt not to resuscitate people - as can individuals themselves in advance - for example, if the individual is extremely frail or has a life-limiting illness.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: This should be done on an individual basis and the use of blanket do not resuscitate orders (DNACPR) is considered unlawful.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: The inquiry says it heard evidence of GPs imposing blanket DNACPRs on care home residents.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: And it pointed to records showing a sharp increase in orders being put in place – they jumped from 16,800 to 26,500 in the first nine months of the pandemic.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: This concern mirrors an earlier Care Quality Commission investigation which found evidence of unacceptable and inappropriate DNACPRs being put in place.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: The impact on staff working in care homes was huge, affecting their mental health and wellbeing, the inquiry said.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: Some moved into the care homes where they worked, in an attempt to protect residents from infection.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: One care home owner in Wales described how 39 staff moved in for a fortnight at the start of the pandemic.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: Seeing so many residents die placed an enormous strain on workers, who often had to provide end-of-life care to multiple people at the same time.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: One care home, for example, lost half of its residents over the course of three weeks.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: Staff told the inquiry of the deep distress they suffered.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: "Staff were sitting on video calls with families, saying their last goodbye to loved ones.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

sentences.text: That was horrendous… staff were crying with the residents, because it was just so emotional for them," one said.
sentences.article_title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says
